title: Electrical Safety and Work at Height
description: Course on electrical safety and work at height: effects of current, protective measures, electrical safety groups, work permits, fall protection systems, rescue and first aid.

sources.title: Labour Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan
Law of the RK “On Civil Protection”
Safety Rules for the Operation of Consumers' Electrical Installations, Order No. 222
Rules for Work with Personnel in Energy Organisations of the RK, Order No. 234
Rules on Occupational Safety and Health for Work at Height, Order No. 109

slides.title: Electrical Safety and Work at Height
body: TRAINING
Practical basics of safely operating electrical installations, work permits and high-level (steeplejack) work
Training course for electrical personnel, steeplejacks and line supervisors

slides.title: After the course you can
body: 01. Recognise electrical and height hazards, assess risks and set safe work boundaries.
02. Correctly use fall protection PPE, dielectric equipment and portable protective earths.
03. Flawlessly perform technical and organisational measures to prepare the worksite and admit crews.
04. Act instantly in incidents: free victims from current, rescue a suspended worker and give first aid.
slides.callout: The course's main goal — zero injuries, no contact with current and prevention of falls from height.

slides.title: Five course parts
body: 01. Electrical safety basics and effects of electric current.
02. Technical safeguards and electrical protective gear.
03. Safe work organisation, electrical safety groups and permits.
04. Safety at height and in high-level (steeplejack) work.
05. Combined work, suspension rescue and first aid.
slides.callout: practical modules of comprehensive safety

slides.title: Electrical safety basics
body: Electric current is invisible, odourless and acts instantly. The only protection is knowing the laws and strictly following the rules.

slides.title: Electrical safety at work
body: Work environment: electrical installations up to and above 1000 V, switchboard rooms, cable routes and switchgear.
Nature of the hazard: electric current shows no outward signs of danger (no colour, smell or sound in normal operation).
Human factor: loss of vigilance, getting used to danger and ignoring the rules cause over 80% of severe electrical injuries.
Main rule: every electrical installation is considered live until proven otherwise and until earthing is in place.
slides.callout: Electric current forgives no mistakes: the lack of visible danger dulls your vigilance!

slides.title: Effects of electric current on the human body
body: Thermal — Severe tissue burns, vessel heating, boiling blood and lymph — Insulation, protective shields, arc-rated PPE
Electrolytic — Decomposition of body fluids, blood breakdown, chemical changes — De-energising, dielectric gloves and insulated tools
Mechanical (dynamic) — Torn muscles, tendons and blood vessels, fractures, dislocations — Automatic disconnection (RCD, fast-acting relays)
Biological — Muscle spasms, cardiac fibrillation, respiratory arrest — Equipotential bonding, TN neutral connection, earthing
slides.callout: Severity depends on the size of the current, the exposure time and its path through the body.

slides.title: 4 thresholds of alternating current (50 Hz)
body: 0.6 — 1.5 mA — Perceptible current: slight tingling, faint itch in the fingers.
10 — 15 mA — Non-let-go current: irresistible muscle spasms, the hand cannot unclench.
50 — 100 mA — Fibrillation current: chaotic heart contractions, circulatory arrest.
> 5 A — Lethal current: instant heart paralysis, the most severe thermal burns.
slides.callout: A current of just 0.1 A (100 mA) for 1–2 seconds is fatal!

slides.title: Local electrical injuries and effects
body: Electrical burns: contact current burns (current passing through tissue) and arc burns (arc temperature reaches 4000–6000 °C).
Electrical marks: firm grey or yellowish spots of dead skin with sharp edges at the current entry and exit points.
Skin metallisation: tiny splashes of molten metal driven into the epidermis by an electric arc.
Electro-ophthalmia: inflammation of the cornea and conjunctiva from intense arc UV radiation (goggles or a face shield required).
slides.callout: Electric arc temperature reaches 6000 °C — working without a face shield and arc suit is deadly!

slides.title: Current paths through the body (current loops)
body: Danger of a current loop: set by the share of total current passing through vital organs — the heart, lungs and brain.
“Hand — hand” loop: ~3.3% of the current passes through the heart. The most common workplace case when touching two phases.
“Left hand — feet” loop: up to 4.0% of the current reaches the heart — the most critical, dangerous path!
“Foot — foot” loop: step voltage current; ~0.4% passes through the heart, but falling to the ground turns it into “hands — feet”.
slides.callout: A fall in the current zone instantly turns the loop from “foot-foot” to the deadly “hands-feet”!

slides.title: CRITICAL BAN: Dangerous approach distances
body: Do not approach unguarded live parts closer than the set minimum distances (up to 1 kV — 0.6 m; 1–35 kV — 0.6 m; 110 kV — 1.0 m; 220 kV — 2.0 m).
Do not work alone in electrical installations where the work permit requires a second person to be present.
Do not touch live insulators and structures without basic electrical protective equipment.
Do not continue work if there are signs of arcing, an unusual transformer hum or a smell of burning.
slides.callout: A person or tool coming closer than permitted causes flashover across the air gap!

slides.title: Premises classified by electrical hazard
body: Premises without increased danger: dry, normal temperature, insulating wooden floors, no conductive dust.
Premises with increased danger: damp (humidity >75%), conductive dust, conductive floors (metal, concrete), temperature >35 °C.
Especially dangerous premises: extreme damp (humidity near 100%), chemically aggressive environment or two signs of increased danger at once.
Outdoor switchgear areas: always equated to the category of especially dangerous premises!
slides.callout: Any work outdoors or in the open air is automatically treated as work in especially dangerous conditions!

slides.title: Touch voltage and step voltage
body: Step voltage: the potential difference between two points on the ground one human step apart (0.8 m).
Current spreading zone: occurs when an OHL wire falls to the ground or on an earth fault. Danger zone radius — 8 metres (indoors 4–5 m).
Potential distribution: falls hyperbolically from the fault point outwards; the largest difference is near the fallen wire.
No hopping on one foot: losing balance and falling onto your hands is deadly, as it creates a “hands — feet” current loop.
slides.callout: The danger radius around a fallen wire is 8 metres! Never approach a wire on the ground!

slides.title: 4 rules for leaving a step voltage zone
body: Feet together — Immediately bring your feet together so there is no potential difference.
“Shuffle” — Move slowly, with the heel of one foot against the toe of the other, never lifting.
Step ≤ 10 cm — Step length must not exceed the foot's width; no wide steps!
Get 8 m away — Keep moving until fully out of the 8-metre danger radius around the fallen wire.
slides.callout: Never run or jump — losing your balance will be fatal!

slides.title: Section I summary: 5 electrical safety barriers
body: 1. Hazard awareness: remember that current is invisible and never be careless in any operation on electrical installations.
2. Distance barrier: strictly keep the minimum permissible distances to live parts.
3. Environmental control: account for humidity, conductive floors and open structures, which cut body resistance tenfold.
4. Behavioural rules: no working alone where the rules require a crew or supervision.
5. Incident readiness: solid knowledge of step voltage and the first aid algorithm for a victim.
slides.callout: Electrical safety is not a set of tips but the law of survival on an industrial site!

slides.title: Technical safeguards
body: Reliable earthing, insulation, extra-low voltage and electrical protective equipment form an impassable technical barrier.

slides.title: Protective earthing: how it works
body: Definition: a deliberate electrical connection of the non-current-carrying metal parts of an installation to an earthing device.
Purpose: to reduce touch voltage to a safe level when phase conductor insulation breaks down to a metal enclosure.
Physical principle: the earth electrode resistance (Re <= 4 Ohm) and the human body (Rb ~ 1000 Ohm) in parallel.
Result: most of the fault current flows to earth through the low-resistance earthing loop, protecting the person.
slides.callout: Current takes the path of least resistance: good earthing takes the hit!

slides.title: Earthing systems of power networks
body: TN-S system: the neutral (N) and protective (PE) conductors are separate throughout the network — the safest system.
TN-C-S system: N and PE functions are combined in one PEN conductor in the upstream part and split at the building entry.
TN-C system: an outdated system with a combined PEN throughout; prohibited for new and reconstructed installations!
TT and IT systems: TT — independent earthing of the installation; IT — isolated neutral with insulation monitoring (mines, mobile units).
slides.callout: Separating PE and N conductors is the key to correct RCD operation and electrical safety!

slides.title: Protective neutral (TN): purpose and tripping
body: TN connection: a deliberate electrical connection of exposed conductive parts to the solidly earthed neutral of the supply via the PE conductor.
Protection principle: turns a phase-to-enclosure fault into a short circuit (SC) between the phase and the protective conductor.
Protection tripping: the short-circuit overcurrent instantly trips the circuit breaker or blows the fuse link.
Standard time: the faulty section of a 220/380 V network must be disconnected within 0.4 seconds (per the PUE).
slides.callout: TN connection turns a fault into a short circuit and cuts the faulty section in a split second!

slides.title: Residual current devices (RCD)
body: Differential transformer: continuously compares the vector sum of currents entering the load via phase and returning via neutral.
Leakage current: when a person touches a live part, a residual current (earth leakage) arises and induces an EMF in the secondary winding.
Tripping threshold: to protect people against direct contact, RCDs with a rated residual current IΔn <= 30 mA are used.
Response speed: a quality RCD disconnects the faulty circuit in 0.02–0.04 seconds, before heart fibrillation sets in.
slides.callout: A 30 mA RCD is the only protection that can save a life in direct contact with a bare wire!

slides.title: Extra-low voltage (ELV / SELV)
body: Definition: rated voltage not exceeding 50 V AC or 120 V DC between conductors or to earth.
Application: supply of portable hand-held power tools and portable lamps in conditions of increased danger.
Voltage levels: 42 V (or 36 V) — in premises with increased danger; 12 V — in especially dangerous conditions (inside boilers, tanks, wells).
Power source: only via isolating step-down transformers with separate windings (autotransformers are prohibited!).
slides.callout: Inside metal tanks and wells, only lamps rated at no more than 12 volts may be used!

slides.title: Electrical protective equipment types
body: Basic up to 1000 V: dielectric gloves, tools with insulated handles, voltage indicators, clamp meters.
Additional up to 1000 V: dielectric overshoes, dielectric mats, insulating stands and covers, protective barriers.
Basic above 1000 V: insulating rods of all types, insulating tongs, voltage indicators above 1000 V.
Additional above 1000 V: dielectric boots, dielectric gloves (above 1 kV they are only additional!), mats.
slides.callout: Basic PPE withstands the operating voltage; additional PPE is used only together with basic PPE!

slides.title: Electrical protective equipment: 4 checks
body: Test stamp — Check the next test date on the stamp. Expired PPE is prohibited!
Visual check — Make sure there are no cracks, punctures, tears, chips or mechanical defects.
Roll test — Roll the glove towards the fingers to check for punctures under air pressure.
Clean and dry — Before work, wipe off dust, dirt, oil and moisture with a clean, dry cloth.
slides.callout: Using electrical protective equipment with an expired test stamp is strictly prohibited!

slides.title: 4 steps to verify absence of voltage
body: Self-check — Check that the indicator works on parts known to be live or with a test device.
Phase by phase — Verify there is no voltage between each phase and earth, then between all phases.
Induced voltage — Make sure there is no dangerous induced voltage from adjacent energised lines and phases.
Re-test — Re-check the indicator on a known live source to rule out a sudden failure.
slides.callout: Always wear dielectric gloves when verifying absence of voltage!

slides.title: Portable protective earthing
body: Purpose: protect workers from voltage applied in error by switching devices and from induced voltage.
Fitting order: FIRST connect the earth clamp to the earthing device (loop), and only THEN to the live parts.
Removal order: strictly in reverse: FIRST take the clamps off the live parts, and only THEN detach the clamp from the earth electrode.
Earthing conductor cross-section: flexible copper wires of at least 16 mm² (up to 1000 V) and at least 25 mm² (above 1000 V) for thermal withstand.
slides.callout: Fitting earths: first to Earth, then to Phase! Removing: first from Phase, then Earth! Wrong order is deadly!

slides.title: Electrical safety signs and posters
body: Prohibition: “DO NOT SWITCH ON! PEOPLE AT WORK”, “DO NOT OPEN! PEOPLE AT WORK” — hung on the drives of switching devices.
Warning: “STOP! HIGH VOLTAGE”, “DO NOT CLIMB! DANGER OF DEATH”, “CAUTION! ELECTRICAL HAZARD” — mark off the danger zone.
Mandatory: “WORK HERE”, “CLIMB HERE” — clearly mark the prepared and verified safe workplace.
Indicative: “EARTHED” — hung on device keys and control handles and on earthed sections of the installation.
slides.callout: The “DO NOT SWITCH ON” sign has the legal force of an order! Only the person who hung it may remove it!

slides.title: CRITICAL BAN: Breaching technical measures
body: Do not start work in an electrical installation without completing all 5 mandatory technical measures to prepare the site.
Do not switch on disconnected devices or remove prohibition signs and mechanical locks without authorisation.
Do not use random wires of non-standard cross-section or twisted wires as portable protective earths.
Do not touch live parts without verifying absence of voltage with a working indicator while wearing dielectric gloves.
slides.callout: De-energising without earthing does not guarantee safety — induced voltage kills just like operating voltage!

slides.title: Work organisation and permits
body: Clearly divided responsibility, strict admission rules and the work permit rule out the human factor and errors.

slides.title: Two ways to authorise electrical work
body: WORK PERMIT: • A written order on a prescribed form.
WORK PERMIT: • Sets the exact place and the start and end times of work.
WORK PERMIT: • Records the crew, responsible persons and safety measures.
WORK PERMIT: • Required for de-energised work and work near live parts.
WORK PERMIT: • Maximum validity — no more than 15 calendar days.
WORK ORDER: • A verbal task for a one-off simple job.
WORK ORDER: • Valid for one work shift of the crew.
WORK ORDER: • Must be recorded in the site operational log.
WORK ORDER: • Done by a small team (1–2 people) with a clear scope.
WORK ORDER: • Used for unplanned urgent minor work up to 1 kV.
slides.callout: Routine operational work follows a pre-approved list, without a work permit or work order.

slides.title: Electrical safety qualification groups
body: Group I: non-electrical staff (office, warehouses, PC operators); briefing once a year, recorded in the log.
Group II: electrotechnological staff (welders, crane operators, machine operators); 72+ hours of training, knows installations up to 1 kV.
Group III: electrical staff; 1–3 months' experience in Group II, may inspect alone and work up to 1 kV.
Group IV: may work in installations above 1 kV and act as work supervisor, permit issuer or person in charge of electrical facilities up to 1 kV.
Group V: highest level (engineers, energy managers, persons in charge of installations above 1 kV); knows all circuits and rules.
slides.callout: A safety group is a personal measure of responsibility and the right to independent access to hazardous work!

slides.title: Persons responsible for safe work
body: Permit issuer (work order giver): decides if work is needed, its safe scope and the qualifications of the crew's responsible persons.
Responsible work manager (RWM): ensures the planned safety measures are complete and sufficient and coordinates the crews.
Permitting officer: responsible for correct workplace preparation, checking absence of voltage, fitting earths and signs.
Work supervisor (WS): responsible for a clear on-site crew briefing, correct use of PPE and continuous supervision.
Observer and crew members: the observer supervises non-electrical staff; crew members strictly follow the WS's instructions.
slides.callout: Each responsible person answers for their part of preparation — combining roles is strictly regulated by the SR!

slides.title: 6 steps to prepare the workplace
body: 1. Disconnection: make the required disconnections with a visible break in the circuit.
2. Locks and signs: lock the drives with LOTO locks and hang prohibition signs.
3. Voltage check: verify absence of voltage on all phases with a working indicator.
4. Earthing: close the fixed earthing switches or apply portable earths.
5. Indicative signs: hang “EARTHED” signs on device keys and handles.
6. Fencing: fence off the workplace with portable screens and hang safety signs.
slides.callout: Strict order of the 6 preparation steps: disconnect → lock → sign → test → earth → fence!

slides.title: LOTO protective lockout in power networks
body: LOTO concept (Lockout / Tagout): mechanical isolation of hazardous energy sources with personal padlocks and warning tags.
Personal lock: each crew member puts their own lock on the breaker or switch lockout device and keeps the only key.
Group lockout: with several crews, a group lock box is used: equipment keys go inside, and every team puts its lock on the box.
Error-proofing: no breaker can be switched on remotely or manually until the last worker removes their personal lock.
slides.callout: One worker — one lock — one key! No one can energise the line while you are working on it!

slides.title: 4 steps to admit a crew under a work permit
body: Staff check — Check the crew by names, ID certificates and electrical safety groups.
Show on site — Prove absence of voltage, show the earths, boundaries and adjacent equipment.
Task briefing — Explain the work method, danger zones, escape routes and safe work practices.
Sign the permit — Permitting officer, work supervisor and crew sign the permit in person.
slides.callout: No work may start without the permitting officer's and work supervisor's signatures on the permit!

slides.title: Continuous supervision during work
body: Duty of the work supervisor (observer): continuously supervise all crew members throughout the task.
No leaving: the work supervisor must not combine supervision with any other work or leave the workplace.
Supervisor's temporary absence: if the work supervisor has to leave, the entire crew must be withdrawn from the installation.
Crew members: may not stay in the switchgear or at height without the work supervisor; switchgear doors are locked during breaks.
slides.callout: The work supervisor is the crew's “safety eyes”: doing their own work means losing control over people!

slides.title: Breaks and completion of work
body: Lunch break: the crew leaves the work zone; the permit stays with the work supervisor; signs, earths and barriers stay in place.
Re-admission after a break: the work supervisor personally checks that the workplace is unchanged and admits the crew without the permitting officer.
Daily end of work: the workplace is tidied up and the permit is handed to the duty operating staff, marked as end of shift.
Final completion: temporary fixtures are dismantled, crew earths removed, and the permit is closed with WS and permitting officer signatures.
slides.callout: After the shift, switching on the installation before the work permit is formally closed is strictly prohibited!

slides.title: 4 work supervisor actions during a break
body: Withdraw crew — Stop the tasks, collect all tools and lead people out of the electrical installation.
Lock access — Lock the switchroom doors, barriers and gates of the work zone.
Keep the setup — Leave all signs, LOTO locks and portable protective earths in place.
Check before re-entry — Before resuming, personally confirm the setup is safe and the earths are intact.
slides.callout: Crew members must not enter the work zone before the work supervisor returns!

slides.title: Admission of seconded staff and contractors
body: Secondment letter: the employer sends an official letter listing the workers, their safety groups and the rights of responsible persons.
Knowledge check: seconded staff receive induction and initial briefings on the client's electrical installation layout.
Admission certificate: issued when a separate fenced work zone is allocated to the contractor on an operating site.
Assigning the permitting officer: initial admission of seconded crews is always done only by the client's own operating staff.
slides.callout: A contractor on site calls for extra attention: initial admission is done only by the owner company's own staff!

slides.title: Section III summary: Organisational control chain
body: Unbroken chain: safety is guaranteed only when every link works — permit, briefing, LOTO and supervision.
Personal responsibility: each worker signs the work permit for their own and their colleagues' safety.
Documenting changes: any change in the crew or work conditions requires the admission to be reissued at once.
Life comes first: organisational rules are based on the analysis of hundreds of real incidents and are mandatory.
slides.callout: A work permit is not a formality but a legal document that protects your life and freedom!

slides.title: Work at height and steeplejack work
body: Falls from height are the leading cause of fatal workplace injuries. The right choice of fall protection saves lives.

slides.title: Work at height defined: regulatory criteria
body: Basic height criterion: work with a risk of falling from 1.3 m (under construction codes) or 1.8 m or more above the surface.
Guarding: work on platforms within 2 m of unguarded drops over 1.3 m, or where guardrails are lower than 1.1 m.
Hazards below: work less than 1.3 m above machines, mechanisms, protruding objects, water or molten metal.
High-level (steeplejack) work: work more than 5 m above the ground or a floor slab, done from erection fixtures or directly from structures.
slides.callout: Even an unprotected fall from just 1.8 metres in 85% of cases leads to disability or death!

slides.title: Fall protection hierarchy: 4 levels
body: Avoidance — Assemble units on the ground before lifting them by crane into position.
Collective guards — Install guardrails, handrails, scaffolds, platforms and safety catch nets.
Restraint — Use a restraint system that physically prevents reaching the edge of a drop.
Fall arrest — A fall arrest system with a harness and energy absorber to safely arrest a fall.
slides.callout: Fall protection PPE is the last line of defence! Collective guards always come first!

slides.title: Safety groups for work at height
body: No group: work from scaffolds, platforms and towers with guardrails of 1.1 m or more, and from leaning ladders up to 5 m.
Group 1: workers admitted to work as part of a crew or under the direct control of an appointed supervisor.
Group 2: foremen, crew leaders, responsible performers and safety specialists who carry out periodic PPE inspections.
Group 3: responsible work managers under permits, persons approving the WEP for work at height, certification board members, rescuers.
slides.callout: A Group 1 worker may not work alone — only under the direct control of a Group 2 or 3 specialist!

slides.title: Two protection systems: Restraint vs Fall arrest
body: RESTRAINT SYSTEM: • Goal: physically PREVENT access to the edge of a drop.
RESTRAINT SYSTEM: • Components: a work belt or harness + a fixed-length lanyard.
RESTRAINT SYSTEM: • No fall: the fall factor is zero (no dynamic shock load).
RESTRAINT SYSTEM: • Load: no energy absorber needed, as a fall is impossible.
RESTRAINT SYSTEM: • Limitation: never use where a fall into a void is possible!
FALL ARREST SYSTEM: • Goal: SAFELY ARREST a fall that has already begun.
FALL ARREST SYSTEM: • Components: full body harness + energy absorber + anchor line.
FALL ARREST SYSTEM: • Shock absorption: the absorber cuts the arrest force to <= 6 kN.
FALL ARREST SYSTEM: • Load distribution: the load is transferred to the thighs, pelvis and chest.
FALL ARREST SYSTEM: • Prerequisite: calculate the clearance below the worker.
slides.callout: A work positioning belt (without shoulder and thigh straps) is PROHIBITED as a fall arrest system!

slides.title: Fall arrest system components: The ABC rule
body: A (Anchor): a reliable anchor device (sling, clamp, beam clamp) with a strength of at least 22 kN (2.2 tonnes).
B (Body wear): a full body harness with shoulder and thigh straps and a dorsal fall arrest D-ring.
C (Connector): a lanyard with an energy absorber, a self-retracting lifeline (SRL) or a rope grab on a flexible line.
100% tie-off rule: when moving along structures, use a twin-leg (Y-shaped) lanyard — one leg is always clipped in!
slides.callout: Fall protection PPE works only with correct anchorage and a calculated clearance!

slides.title: Fall factor and clearance
body: Fall factor = Fall height / Lanyard length. It determines how hard the dynamic shock on the worker's body is in a fall.
Factor 0 (anchor above head): the best option, minimal fall distance, gentle absorber deployment.
Factor 1 (anchor at chest/shoulder level): a standard fall of the slack lanyard length; acceptable with an energy absorber.
Factor 2 (anchor at foot level): CRITICAL risk! Free fall equals twice the lanyard length (up to 4 m); risk of hitting structures.
Clearance: the calculated distance below the workplace (lanyard length + absorber extension 1.2 m + height 1.8 m + margin 1.0 m = 5.7–6.0 m).
slides.callout: Clip the lanyard AS HIGH ABOVE YOUR HEAD AS POSSIBLE! Factor 2 — extreme load on the anchor and spine!

slides.title: Anchor devices and rigid / flexible lines
body: Class A: fixed structural anchor points on concrete and steel load-bearing building structures.
Class B: portable temporary anchor devices (textile slings, tripods, I-beam clamps).
Class C: flexible horizontal cable anchor lines for free, continuous movement of the worker along the structure.
Class D: rigid horizontal rail anchor lines with a sliding trolley for heavy-duty use.
Never anchor to unreliable supports: process pipelines, cable trays, radiators and window frames!
slides.callout: Never attach the lanyard to process pipes or cable trays — only to verified load-bearing structures!

slides.title: Ladders, stepladders and access platforms
body: Three points of contact rule: when climbing up or down a ladder, always keep two hands and one foot (or two feet and one hand) on it.
Leaning ladder angle: strictly 70–75 degrees to the horizontal (height-to-base ratio 4:1).
Top end: a leaning ladder must extend at least 1.0 metre above the landing.
Work ban: do not work from the top two steps of stepladders without handrails and guarded platforms.
No heavy work: heavy erection and power electrical installation work must not be done from leaning ladders.
slides.callout: A leaning ladder is a means of access, not a workplace! Heavy work is done only from scaffolds and platforms!

slides.title: 4 steps of a pre-use harness check
body: Webbing — Check the webbing for cuts, burns, abrasion and intact contrast stitching.
Metal hardware — Inspect D-rings and buckles for deformation, cracks, corrosion and secure latches.
Fall indicator — Make sure the fabric fall indicator is intact (the harness has not arrested a fall).
Body fit — Adjust the thigh and shoulder straps: a flat hand should fit snugly under the thigh strap.
slides.callout: A harness that has arrested a fall is immediately withdrawn from use and destroyed!

slides.title: Risk matrix for erection work at height
body: Person falling from height — Severe multiple trauma, spinal fractures, death — 100% tie-off, Y-lanyard, horizontal anchor line
Falling objects and tools — Injury to personnel at ground level — Helmets, protective canopies, tool lanyards, 15 cm toe boards
Scaffold/platform instability — Collapse of the structure with people and materials — Anchoring to the facade, diagonal bracing, formal acceptance
Weather (wind, thunderstorm, ice) — Blown off by a gust, loss of balance, slipping, lightning strike — Monitor forecasts, stop work at once if wind >10–12 m/s
slides.callout: The danger zone below work at height must be fenced off with warning tape and signs!

slides.title: CRITICAL BAN: Violations during work at height
body: Being at height without a correctly worn and adjusted full body harness and a locked carabiner.
Wind speed above 10–12 m/s (when erecting solid structures and panels) or 15 m/s for ordinary work.
Onset of a thunderstorm, squall, fog (visibility under 50 m) or icing of structures and ladders.
No approved work execution plan for work at height (WEP) or rescue and evacuation plan (REP).
Using homemade, uncertified or damaged platforms, barrels or stands instead of scaffolding.
slides.callout: An unprotected fall gives no second chance — safety at height is absolute!

slides.title: Combined work, rescue and first aid
body: Specifics of electrical work at height, preventing suspension trauma, emergency evacuation and first aid for victims.

slides.title: 4 safety steps for work on OHL poles
body: Pole check — Check for wood rot or cracks in reinforced concrete, pole stability and guy wires.
100% tie-off — Use a flexible anchor line or a pole strap throughout the climb.
Safety zone — Keep safe clearances to adjacent lines that are live or carry induced voltage.
Earth the line — Fit portable earths on both sides of the worksite on all phase conductors.
slides.callout: Climbing angle poles from the inside of the conductor angle is strictly prohibited!

slides.title: Aerial work platforms (AWP) near OHL
body: Work permit: work within 30 metres of the outermost OHL conductor is done only under a work permit and a manager's supervision.
Chassis earthing: the AWP vehicle body must be earthed with a flexible copper conductor to a fixed earth electrode or the substation earth.
100% tie-off: an electrician in the basket must be clipped by the harness lanyard to the basket's dedicated certified anchor point.
No travel: moving the AWP with people in the basket or with the boom raised is strictly prohibited!
slides.callout: Earthing the AWP body and clipping into the basket are mandatory before switching on the boom hydraulics!

slides.title: 4 stages of the rescue plan (REP)
body: Alarm and timer — Alert the supervisor at once and start timing. Rescue time — up to 10 minutes!
Rig rescue kit — Attach the rescue device to a secure anchor above the victim or on an adjacent structure.
Hook and lower — Clip the rescue line to the suspended worker's harness, cut their lanyard, lower gently.
Shock control — Place them in the right position (sitting or semi-sitting!), call an ambulance.
slides.callout: The rescue and evacuation plan (REP) and rescue kit must be on site before work starts!

slides.title: Suspension trauma in a harness
body: Injury mechanism: thigh straps compress the femoral veins and blood pools in the legs, causing acute venous congestion.
Reduced blood return: after 5–10 minutes of motionless hanging, brain hypoxia, loss of consciousness and cardiac arrest follow.
Self-help while suspended: if conscious, actively move the legs (“pedal a bicycle”) and stand in the foot-loop stirrups.
GOLDEN RULE: after lowering, NEVER lay the victim flat on their back! (risk of “reflow syndrome” and cardiac arrest).
slides.callout: After lowering the victim, NEVER, EVER LAY THEM ON THEIR BACK! Keep them semi-sitting for 30+ minutes to spare the heart from toxic shock!

slides.title: Releasing a victim from current at height
body: Step 1. De-energise the installation: switch off the nearest isolator, breaker or switch with the emergency stop.
Step 2. Prevent a fall: remember that once the current is off, the victim will go limp and fall unless secured by fall protection!
Step 3. Insulate the rescuer: if power cannot be cut quickly, use dielectric gloves, an insulating rod or an axe with a dry handle.
Step 4. Separate the victim: pull the victim by dry clothing only, with one hand, without touching bare skin or metal.
slides.callout: When cutting the current to a victim at height, secure them from falling: the fall after a shock is deadlier than the current!

slides.title: First aid: cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)
body: Assessment: check consciousness (call out, shake the shoulders) and breathing (the “listen — look — feel” rule for 10 seconds).
Chest compressions: 30 presses on the centre of the breastbone, 5–6 cm deep, at 100–120 per minute with the heel of the hand.
Rescue breaths: 2 mouth-to-mouth breaths through a barrier face shield after tilting the head back and pinching the nose.
Using an AED (defibrillator): apply the automated defibrillator pads and follow the device's voice prompts.
Fractures and bleeding: apply a pressure bandage to bleeding, splint fractures, do not reset bone fragments!
slides.callout: Start CPR immediately! Every minute of delay cuts the brain's chance of survival by 10%! Ratio: 30 to 2!

slides.title: CRITICAL STOP: 6 grounds for an absolute stop
body: 1. Sudden appearance of voltage on disconnected live parts or sparking at the worksite.
2. Worsening weather: onset of a thunderstorm, squall wind (>12 m/s), snowstorm or dense fog.
3. Detection of a defect or tear in the harness, lanyard, carabiner or anchor line during work.
4. Sudden illness of any crew member (dizziness, nausea, weakness, chest pain).
5. Forced departure of the work supervisor or the person providing continuous supervision.
6. An emergency, or tools or structures falling near people.
slides.callout: The right to stop work (“STOP CARD”) is every worker's sacred right, with no risk of punishment!

slides.title: Final admission checklist: 6 safety conditions
body: Work permit issued — Permit signed by all parties, still valid, task briefing given.
De-energised and earthed — Switching devices off, absence of voltage verified, earths applied.
LOTO lockout in place — Personal mechanical locks on the drives, keys held by crew members.
Electrical PPE checked — Dielectric gloves, tools and indicators tested, stamps valid.
Full body harness fitted — 100% continuous tie-off, anchor point reliable (>=22 kN), twin-leg lanyard connected.
Rescue plan ready — Evacuation kit on site, communications working, danger zone below fenced off.
